name: Sakurajima
label: Sakurajima
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '城山公園展望台' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1280125814: the OpenStreetMap point 'Sakurajima'.
notes: Active volcano island reached by a short ferry ride.

text.description: Sakurajima is the smoking volcano that sits across the bay from Kagoshima city, and it is the picture most people come here to take. Its summit has three peaks, and the highest, Kita-dake, rises to 1,117 m. The volcano is only about 4 km from the city across the water, so a single frame can hold the rooftops, the bay and the mountain together. It has been erupting almost constantly since 1955, so a small plume of ash is often part of the view. It was once a true island. The huge 1914 eruption sent lava into the narrow strait and joined it to the mainland, which is why it is now called a peninsula. The best-known view is from the Shiroyama Park observation deck, which looks over the city and Kagoshima Bay with the volcano rising behind the water. Guides treat it as the best free panorama in town. Early morning is usually the clearest, with fewer people, and the city lights after dark are also popular. Ash and haze are common, so look at the sky before you climb. If you want the volcano bigger in the frame, the Sakurajima ferry terminal gives a closer view, while the Sengan-en garden frames the volcano as a backdrop behind the garden.
text.geographic_location: Sakurajima lies in Kagoshima Bay (Kinkō-wan), directly across the water from central Kagoshima city. The best-known viewpoint is on the hill of Shiroyama, above the city.
text.directions_text: Start from central Kagoshima city and head up to Shiroyama Park, either by the city sightseeing bus or on foot (the climb is steep). The observation deck is at the top of the Shiroyama promenade. To see Sakurajima close up instead, take the Sakurajima Ferry across the bay. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic city, bay and volcano frame. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the peaks closer and to pick out any ash plume. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground, because the volcano will look smaller.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The subject is Sakurajima itself. The Shiroyama Park observation deck (城山公園展望台), at the top of the Shiroyama promenade, is an alternative viewpoint across the bay. From the deck, Sakurajima rises across the water behind the city and Kagoshima Bay, so you can frame the city below and the volcano above it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the lower third line, so that the volcano and sky fill most of the frame. Keep a strip of city and bay at the bottom for scale. For a closer, more dramatic volcano, use the view from the Sakurajima ferry terminal as an alternative. The Sengan-en garden is another option, with the volcano as a backdrop behind the garden.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the volcano to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and ash plume keep their detail. In hazy conditions, a small boost in contrast when editing can help. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the city lights sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before haze and crowds build up. The night city lights are a good second choice.

text.access_note: The Shiroyama observation deck is described in guides as a free viewpoint open all day, but check the official site before you go; Sengan-en is a ticketed garden, so check the official site there too.

name: Sengan-en
label: Sengan-en Garden
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1309677433: the OpenStreetMap point 'Sengan-En'.
notes: Shimazu clan's villa garden with Sakurajima as borrowed scenery.

text.description:
Sengan-en is a Japanese garden attached to a former residence of the Shimazu clan in Kagoshima. It is a designated Place of Scenic Beauty. Together with the neighbouring Shōko Shūseikan, it forms part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution: Iron and Steel, Shipbuilding and Coal Mining'. The garden is managed by Shimadzu Ltd.

It photographs well because the designers used the view of Sakurajima across Kagoshima Bay as 'borrowed scenery', so the volcano becomes the backdrop to the ponds, paths and planting. That gives you a layered picture, with garden in front and bay and mountain behind.

The residence was built by Shimazu Mitsuhisa in 1658. In 1736 Shimazu Yoshitaka added a winding water feature (a kyokusui) and moso bamboo that came from China by way of the Ryūkyū Kingdom. In the Bakumatsu and Meiji periods it hosted visiting dignitaries, including Harry Smith Parkes in 1866 and Edward VIII in 1922.

For your phone, look for a foreground such as water, a lantern or foliage, then let Sakurajima fill the top of the frame. Walk a little between pictures, because small changes in position make a big difference to how the garden and the mountain line up.
text.geographic_location: Sengan-en is in Kagoshima, Kagoshima Prefecture, next to the Shōko Shūseikan, and its gardens borrow the view of Sakurajima across Kagoshima Bay.
text.directions_text: Check local transport options before you go. From it you look south. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the garden and the bay together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) in tighter spots to fit in a pond or path. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring Sakurajima closer and to pick out details such as lanterns or bamboo.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 120 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Take a few photos here, then walk towards the garden and try different positions.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon or the line of the bay on the upper third. Keep something from the garden in the lower part of the frame so the picture has depth. If the volcano is visible, leave it room at the top rather than cropping it tight.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the garden to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Try portrait mode for close-ups of leaves, lanterns or bamboo. Live Photos can capture moving water or leaves.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or later in the afternoon usually gives softer light on the garden and a gentler sky behind the volcano than the middle of the day.

text.access_note: Sengan-en is a managed garden that may be ticketed with set opening times, so check the official site before you go.

name: Shiroyama Observation Deck
label: Shiroyama Viewpoint
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3051317914: the OpenStreetMap point 'Mt. Shiroyama'.
notes: Best panorama of the city with Sakurajima across the bay.

text.description:
Shiroyama point. The hill is small, with a true height of 107 m. It was originally called Tsuru ga mine (鶴ヶ峯). It is best known as the place where the Battle of Shiroyama was fought in 1877, the closing episode of the Satsuma rebellion, so many visitors come for the history as well as the view.

For photographs, the appeal is height. On a clear day the view may extend over parts of the city, giving you a wide scene rather than a single building or street. If there are branches or a railing at the edge of the frame, you can use them to add depth.

Practical advice: allow a few minutes to look around before choosing your angle, because the view can change noticeably even a few steps to either side. Keep your lens clean, since a smudged phone lens is the most common reason for hazy distance shots. If the sky is bright and the land below is darker, tap on the distance and lower the exposure slightly. Check current local information before you go in case there are any access notices for the area.
text.geographic_location: The spot is on Mount Shiroyama, a low hill within Kagoshima city in Kagoshima Prefecture, Japan.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so head to Mount Shiroyama in Kagoshima and look for the Shiroyama Observation Deck. The phone icon on the map is about 70 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the scene and sky in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out single details in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 70 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Face north to photograph the hill itself, then turn around to see what view opens out.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, depending on whether the sky or the land below is more interesting. If there are branches or a railing at the edge of the frame, use them to give a sense of depth. Hold the phone level, because a tilted horizon is obvious in a wide view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the part of the view you care about and slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. For a sweeping view, try panorama mode, moving slowly and keeping the phone steady. Use the 0.5x lens for tight spots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: A clear day gives the longest view. Morning or late afternoon usually brings softer light than midday. Check the weather before you go.

text.access_note: Access arrangements for the hill and any viewing area may vary, so check current local information before you go.

name: Kagoshima Aquarium
label: Kagoshima Aquarium
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/196458884: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kagoshima City Aquarium' (150 m across).
notes: Waterfront aquarium known for whale sharks and dolphins.

text.description: Kagoshima Aquarium is a large public aquarium that opened on 30 May 1997. It shows sea life from the Kagoshima coast, the Kuroshio current and Kagoshima Bay, plus some river and brackish-water species. The building's appearance is based on a stingray. Inside, the route runs over five floors from the basement up. The best-known residents are the whale sharks in the big Kuroshio tank, which hold 1,500,000 litres of water. The fifth-floor Observation Hall looks across the bay to Sakurajima, which makes a good second picture from the same visit. It is about 50 m west of the centre of the building, which is around 150 m across, so you will be close to its edge and will not be able to fit all of it in. Keep the horizon level and leave some sky above the roofline. If the entrance area is busy, wait a moment for a gap between groups. Inside, tanks are dim and the fish keep moving, so take several frames and keep the best. Reflections from the glass are a common problem, so stand close to the tank and avoid bright lights behind you.
text.geographic_location: In the city of Kagoshima, on the shore of Kagoshima Bay, with Sakurajima on the far side of the water.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app to head for the aquarium, which is on the bay side of Kagoshima. Walk east from it towards the building. The phone icon on the map is about 15 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in as much of the long building as you can from close range, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tighter, less stretched view. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for details such as the entrance or signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 15 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. The building lies to the east, directly in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the roofline with a horizontal grid line so the building does not look tilted. Keep the phone level, as tilting it up distorts the edges, especially at 0.5x. Include a little foreground, such as paving or planting, to give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls do not turn out too dark. Indoors, tap on the brightest part of a tank and keep the phone steady. Live Photos can help catch a fish or whale shark at the right moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. Because you are shooting east from where you stand, the afternoon sun will be behind you, which should light the side of the building facing you.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for opening times and entry rules.

name: Museum of the Meiji Restoration
label: Meiji Restoration Mus.
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/117143629: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museum of the Meiji Restoration' (83 m across).
notes: Museum about the Satsuma role in the Meiji Restoration.

text.description: The Museum of the Meiji Restoration (Ishin-furusato-kan) is a history museum in Kagoshima, set beside the Kōtsuki River. Inside, the basement hall uses sound, light and robots to tell the story of the Meiji Restoration, while the first floor looks at the people, things and events of Satsuma Province. That makes it a useful place to pair a quick outside photo with a longer visit if you have time. The outline of the site is fairly large, about 83 metres across, so you will want to step back a little to fit it in. Start with a wide view of the main frontage, then move closer for details such as signs, entrances and the way the building sits next to the water. Keep an eye on people walking through the frame; a short wait usually gives you a cleaner shot. If you plan to go inside, remember that photography rules can differ between galleries, so look for signs at the door and ask staff if you are unsure.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Kagoshima, on the bank of the Kōtsuki River. It sits in the riverside area of the city and is easy to place on the map by the water.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Use the map to reach the museum beside the Kōtsuki River. Once there, head to the phone icon on the map, which is right at the museum itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the building, and switch to the default lens (1x) when you have room to step back.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Then move back or to the side as needed to frame the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the roofline up with a horizontal grid line so the building does not lean. Try one wide shot of the whole frontage, then a closer one of the entrance or a detail. If the river is visible, include a strip of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the walls keep their detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the light is even, is the easiest for a clear shot of the whole front. Early morning is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: This is a museum, so entry may be ticketed and hours may vary; check the official site before you go.

name: Kagoshima Castle
label: Tsurumaru Castle
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3089086539: the OpenStreetMap point 'Kagoshima Castle'.
notes: Moated Shimazu castle ruins with a rebuilt gate and stone walls.

text.description: Kagoshima Castle, known locally as Tsurumaru Castle, was not a tall-towered fortress. It was built as a large fortified residence by Shimazu Tadatsune and finished in 1604, with moats and low walls but no keep and no high stone walls. That shapes the photos: you are capturing a wide, calm historic site rather than a tower, so think of the setting and the gateway. Much of the original burned down in the 1870s, and the grounds are now home to Reimeikan (the prefectural history centre) and other museums. A reconstruction of the Otemon main gate, built from surviving documents and photographs, was completed in 2020 and gives you the clearest 'castle' subject. The ruins have been a National Historic Site since 2023, and Mount Shiroyama rises behind the castle to the north, which can add a green backdrop. Start by stepping back far enough to fit the whole gate or wall in one frame, then move closer for details such as stonework. Keep your phone level so the long horizontal lines stay straight. If the grounds are busy, wait a moment for a gap rather than cropping people out afterwards.
text.geographic_location: In central Kagoshima city, on the flat ground below Mount Shiroyama, with Kinko Bay to the south. The castle site now includes Reimeikan and nearby museums.
text.directions_text: Mount Shiroyama is to the north of the castle and Kinko Bay to the south, which helps you orient yourself. The phone icon on the map is about 80 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate or wall as you see it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want the gate or wall and the sky together. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof details and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 80 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. Face north-west towards the castle point. Take a few steps either side to avoid people or railings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the wall or gate along a horizontal line so it does not slope. Put something in the foreground to give the scene depth. Take one wide shot for the setting and one closer shot of the gate or stonework. Keep the sky about a third of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate or wall to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its colour and the stonework stays dark enough to show texture. Wipe the lens before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. In the morning the sun is behind you as you face north-west, so the front of the site is lit. Midday can look flat and harsh.

text.access_note: Parts of the castle grounds and the museums may have their own entry rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Terukuni Shrine
label: Terukuni Shrine
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Terukuni Shrine' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1412930611: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Terukuni shrine' (194 m across).
notes: Shrine dedicated to Shimazu Nariakira at the foot of Shiroyama.

text.description:
Terukuni Shrine is a Shinto shrine in the middle of Kagoshima city. It honours Shimazu Nariakira, whose posthumous name, Terukuni Daimyōjin, gives the shrine its name. It was founded in 1882, in the Meiji period, and belongs to a very small class of shrines set up to venerate people who were ordinary subjects of the Emperor in life.

For a phone photo, the best subject is the pruned tree on the approach. It is trimmed into the shape of a bird with its wings spread, and it is the shrine's most distinctive feature. Frame it with the worship hall behind and you get a picture that is clearly this shrine and no other.

A second picture is worth taking at the large white torii gate. It stands over a road, so a low angle looking up makes it tower against the city streets behind. Keep out of the carriageway and shoot from the pavement.

Be considerate of worshippers. Keep out of their way, and do not photograph the inner hall, where restrictions may apply. Early morning is usually quieter and gives softer light, while late afternoon gives warmer light.
text.geographic_location: Terukuni Shrine is in the city of Kagoshima, in Kagoshima Prefecture. It sits among the downtown streets, and its large white torii gate stands over a road.
text.directions_text: Find Terukuni Shrine by name on a map and head there from central Kagoshima city. Once there, walk in through the torii and along the approach to the pruned tree, which is the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the bird-shaped tree with the worship hall behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the torii gate from a low angle. Telephoto (2x or more) can pick out details of the tree or hall without you walking up to them.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the tree, with its outstretched wings, sits in front of the worship hall. For the alternative view, shoot the large white torii gate from the pavement. Do not stand in the road beneath it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the tree on one of the vertical lines, with the roof of the hall behind it. Keep the phone fairly low so the wings stand out against the building. For the torii, crouch, tilt the phone up and use 0.5x so the gate towers above the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tree to focus. If the sky is bright, drag the exposure slider down a little so the tree and hall stay dark enough to show detail. Take a few frames, because people walk through the approach.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning for softer light and fewer people, or late afternoon for warmer, golden-hour light.

text.access_note: Photography is generally allowed in the grounds, but check the official site before you go, and keep out of worshippers' way and away from the inner hall.
claims_not_in_sources: The pruned tree on the approach is trimmed to look like a bird with spread wings.
The large white torii gate stands over a road, with the downtown streetscape behind it.
Early morning is quieter with softer light, and late afternoon gives golden-hour light.
Photography is generally allowed, but photographing the inner hall may be restricted.

name: Amuran
label: Amuran Ferris Wheel
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2144219417: the OpenStreetMap point 'アミュラン'.
notes: Rooftop Ferris wheel above Kagoshima-Chūō Station.

text.description:
Amuran is the big Ferris wheel that sits on the roof of Amu Plaza Kagoshima, right beside Kagoshima-Chūō Station. It is one of the city's best-known attractions, and it works well in photographs because it gives you a clear, round shape against the sky, with the Amu Plaza building underneath it. That makes it easy to place the wheel in a wider scene of everyday city life.

The wheel is 60 m across and reaches 91 m above the ground at its highest point. It has 36 gondolas, two of which are fully transparent, and one full turn takes about 14 and a half minutes. It opened in September 2004, and by May 2007 it had carried more than a million riders. The slow turn means you can wait a moment for a bright gondola to reach a pleasing spot in your frame.

Keep the phone level and use the gridlines so the building's edges stay straight. If other people are passing, wait for a gap, or include them to show the scale of the place. A second shot from inside a gondola is possible if you ride, but check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Amuran is in central Kagoshima, on top of the Amu Plaza Kagoshima shopping building, which adjoins Kagoshima-Chūō Station.
text.directions_text: Head for Amu Plaza Kagoshima beside Kagoshima-Chūō Station. The wheel is on the roof, so it is easy to spot once you are close. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which fits the whole wheel from where you stand. If you want the building and the street in the picture too, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). For a tighter shot of the gondolas, use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Kagoshima-Chuo Station East Exit Station Square (east exit side of the station, facing Amu Plaza). A street-level view of the Amu Plaza building and its rooftop Ferris wheel, framed by the station front and nearby skyscrapers.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the wheel's centre near one of the crossing points, leaving a little sky around the rim. Keep the phone upright and level so the building doesn't lean. Zoom in to 2x or more to fill the frame with the wheel and its gondolas.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wheel to focus, then slide the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright and the wheel looks dark. In the evening, try night mode and hold the phone still against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight with a clear sky shows the wheel's shape most cleanly. Around dusk, when the sky is deep blue and the wheel may be lit, is a good time to try night mode.

text.access_note: The wheel is part of a shopping complex and riding is likely to need a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Looking west from the stand-here point, the wheel should be visible above the Amu Plaza building.
The wheel may be lit after dark.
Riding the wheel is likely to need a ticket.

name: Kagoshima Prefectural Museum of Culture Reimeikan
label: Reimeikan Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/7452097: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Reimeikan, Kagoshima Prefectural Center for Historical Material' (194 m across).
notes: History museum inside the old castle grounds.

text.description:
Reimeikan is the Kagoshima prefectural museum of history and culture, and it stands in the grounds of Tsurumaru Castle in Kagoshima. It opened in 1983 and shows material about the history and culture of Kagoshima Prefecture. The museum site is large, and the whole outline is nearly 200 metres across. That makes it a good subject for broad, calm photographs of a big public site set among old castle ground.

The castle setting is what makes the picture. You are in a historic site, so the museum can be framed with the castle grounds around it. Take a few wide shots first to show how big the site is, then try a few closer frames of whatever catches your eye.

Because the phone icon on the map is at the centre of the museum outline, you can walk around the grounds to find a clean angle. Keep your phone level so the straight lines in your frame do not lean. If other visitors are in the way, wait a moment for a clear view. Before you go, check the official site for opening times.
text.geographic_location: Reimeikan is in Kagoshima, inside the grounds of Tsurumaru Castle.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Tsurumaru Castle grounds in Kagoshima and follow the map. Once you are in the castle grounds, the phone icon on the map is at the centre of the museum outline, so follow the map from there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the large site into the frame, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details that catch your eye.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Then move around the grounds to find an angle that fits the museum in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use them to keep your shot level so it does not lean. Include some of the castle grounds around the museum to give a sense of scale. Try one wide shot and one closer shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the museum to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the walls do not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer.

text.access_note: Check the official site for opening hours and admission before you go.

name: Ishibashi Park
label: Ishibashi Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '西田橋' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '西田橋' (way/733863541): middle (76 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/19988857: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ishibashi Park' (403 m across).
notes: Park with historic stone arch bridges moved from the Kōtsuki River.

text.description:
Ishibashi Park is a small riverside park in Kagoshima that keeps three of the old Edo-period stone bridges. They were built to carry the roads over the Kōtsuki River. Two of the original five collapsed in the floods of August 1993. The three that survived were moved here, restored, and opened as a park in 2000. For a phone photographer the appeal is simple: carefully cut stone arches in the foreground, and Sakurajima rising across Kinko Bay behind them.

The bridge to aim for is 西田橋 (Nishida-bashi), a four-arch bridge. Daimyō lords used it on their journeys to and from Edo, which is why so much was spent on it. Also in the park is 旧高麗橋 (Kōrai-bashi), a second four-arch bridge. Tamae-bashi, now the one closest to the sea, keeps most of the original features of the stone bridges. There is also a statue of Iwanaga Sangorō, the mason who built the five bridges, and a reconstructed wooden gate, 西田橋御門, which gives a period-drama feel to a wider shot.

Keep the arches and the volcano in the same frame and let the water fill the lower part of the picture. The volcano only shows when the weather is clear, so check the forecast. One guide suggests the afternoon, when the light falls on the bridge from the front rather than from behind.
text.geographic_location: Ishibashi Park is in the Hama-machi area of Kagoshima, at the mouth of the Inari River beside National Route 10. It looks out over the water towards Sakurajima.
text.directions_text: Start from Kagoshima-Chuo Station or Kagoshima Station. It is about 10 to 15 minutes on foot, so allow a little extra. Head for the waterfront and National Route 10, then look for the stone bridges and the museum building beside them. Once you are in the park, look for the walkway near 西田橋. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the four arches and Sakurajima into one frame. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to make the volcano look larger behind the bridge. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only for the wooden gate or the full length of a bridge from close up.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 西田橋 (shot from the walkway a short distance from the bridge, looking toward the water and Sakurajima). The four-arch Edo-era stone bridge with Sakurajima volcano rising across Kinko Bay in the background. On the walkway near the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the water line level. Put the bridge arches in the lower half and leave the volcano's outline clear above them. For a second picture, step across to 旧高麗橋, the other four-arch bridge, with Sakurajima behind it. Or turn to 西田橋御門, the large reconstructed wooden gate, for a more traditional feel.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the volcano to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stone does not look washed out. If the haze hides the volcano, try the telephoto lens rather than a wider one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Afternoon, when, according to one guide, the light falls on the bridge from the front. Choose a clear day, since Sakurajima may not show in cloud or haze.

text.access_note: Opening arrangements and rules for photography may differ, so check the official site before you go.

name: Kagoshima Spinning Mill
label: Spinning Mill
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '旧鹿児島紡績所技師館（異人館）' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: '仙巌園（礒庭園）前' (pois).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q38276680: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Early Meiji brick mill and the former British engineers' house.

text.description:
This is the old residence built for the British engineers who came to set up Satsuma's cotton mill, and it is the surviving building of the Kagoshima Spinning Mill site. It was finished in 1867: a two-storey wooden house, painted white, with open verandahs on its front. It covers about 344 square metres. The engineers went home after only a year, and the house later served as a cannon-factory office and, in 1877, as a temporary hospital during the Satsuma Rebellion. It was moved to the grounds of Kagoshima Castle in 1884 and returned to its original spot in 1936. The wider mill site is now part of the Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, a UNESCO World Heritage listing from 2015.

It photographs well because the building is simple and clear: pale walls, regular verandah arches and a calm garden in front. Nothing else competes with it, so you can keep the picture clean. The best shot is of the outside, as interior photography is not allowed. Take a few steps back from the verandahs so both floors fit in the frame, and keep the vertical lines straight. If you have time, also take a closer picture of the verandah rhythm, where the repeated posts and railings make a pleasing pattern. The mill itself no longer stands, and the residence is the surviving building, with only a memorial plaque at the mill site. Come for the house itself, and give yourself a few quiet minutes in the front yard.
text.geographic_location: In the Yoshino neighbourhood of Kagoshima city, about 300 m from the Sengan-en area. The site of the old mill itself lies close by.
text.directions_text: There are no railway or tram stops listed close by. The residence is about 300 m from the Sengan-en area. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which gives a natural view of the whole facade. If the front yard is too shallow to fit both floors and the verandahs, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) and keep the phone level so the walls do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (from the front yard (前庭) facing the facade). The two-storey wooden colonial-style building with its open verandahs, framed from the front yard. The old mill site lies to the south-west of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the verandah posts with the vertical lines so the house looks straight. Keep the whole facade in the frame with a little sky and a little lawn. For a second view, the walk in from Ishibashi Memorial Park (石橋記念公園) gives a different approach to the building. Take all photos from outside, because interior photography is prohibited.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the paint keeps its detail. Take a couple of frames at 1x and 0.5x so you can choose later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit in daylight, when the light is even and the white walls look clean. Overcast skies also work well for a building this pale.

text.access_note: The residence is a protected heritage building and interior photography is prohibited, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.
claims_not_in_sources: The front yard may be too shallow to fit both storeys at 1x, so the ultra-wide (0.5x) can help.
Even daylight or an overcast sky suits the white walls, and direct bright sun may make them harder to expose.
